title: Soils and Soil Conservation - India and Andhra Pradesh
intake_rule: Every printed page was read once from its rendered image. Printed prose, figures, maps, lists and PYQs were recorded before textbook integration. Handwritten annotations were ignored.
table_policy: Every printed grid or structured list is preserved cell-by-cell. Verified corrections are labelled separately; concepts are explained in prose and comparisons remain responsive semantic tables.

pages.heading: Soil definition, formation factors and physical constituents

facts.claim: Soil is the natural material at the land surface that supports rooted plants and develops through interactions among parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time.
Pedogenesis is soil formation; the book's claim of roughly 200-400 years for 1 cm of soil is only a broad teaching estimate, not a universal formation rate.
The book prints an idealised composition of 45% mineral matter, 25% water, 25% air and 5% organic matter; actual proportions vary with texture, structure and moisture.

Passive factors printed are parent material and time; active factors printed are climate, organisms, topography/relief and human activity, but modern summaries treat all five CLORPT factors as interacting controls.
Humus is the relatively stable dark organic fraction formed through decomposition; it affects aggregation, nutrient retention and water relations.
Soil texture is the relative proportion of sand, silt and clay; particle-size limits depend on the classification system and the printed limits must not be universalised.
The book lists clay below 0.002 mm, sand about 0.05-2 mm and silt between clay and sand; the exact silt lower limit is system-specific.
Soil structure describes the arrangement of primary particles into aggregates or peds.
Soil water occupies pore spaces, dissolves and transports solutes and is partly available to plants; availability depends on retention and matric forces.
Soil air occupies pores not filled by water and is essential for root and microbial respiration.

pages.heading: Soil aeration, reaction, colour, horizons and transport

facts.claim: Well-aerated soil supports aerobic organisms; prolonged saturation limits oxygen and favours anaerobic conditions.
Oxidation-reduction conditions influence colour, especially iron-related red, brown and grey mottles.
Soil reaction is expressed as pH; pH 7 is neutral, values below 7 acidic and above 7 alkaline, not the book's incorrect 7.2 threshold.
Many crops perform well over a moderately acidic to neutral range, but optimum pH is crop- and soil-specific; 6.5-7.5 is not universal.
The book's printed soil-temperature range of 5-10 degrees is not a general property; soil temperature varies by climate, season, depth, cover and moisture.
Soil depth affects rooting volume and water storage; the printed 50 cm crop-suitability threshold is not universal.
Soil colour reflects organic matter, minerals, drainage and oxidation state; black colour does not by itself prove fertility.
A soil horizon is a layer approximately parallel to the surface with properties different from adjacent layers; a soil profile is the vertical sequence of horizons.
The printed profile shows O, A, E, B, C and R: organic surface; mineral topsoil; eluviation; illuvial accumulation; partly altered parent material; and bedrock.
Residual (in-situ) soils form mainly over their parent material; transported soils are moved by water, wind, ice or gravity before deposition.

The older zonal-interzonal-azonal system grouped soils by dominant climate/vegetation, local parent-material or drainage controls, and weak profile development/transport respectively; it is historical, not current Soil Taxonomy.
The book attributes an 1893 fourfold Indian-soil grouping to Voelcker: alluvial, black, red and laterite.
The printed ICAR grouping lists eight broad soil groups: alluvial; black; red and yellow; laterite; forest/mountain; arid/desert; saline/alkaline; and peaty/marshy.
Alluvial soils are widespread in the northern plains and river valleys and occur in deltas and coastal plains; percentages and area figures are date- and classification-specific.
Alluvium is deposited by flowing water and may range from sand to clay; it is not uniformly fertile or uniformly textured.
Alluvial soils commonly vary in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter, while potash or lime status varies; a blanket nutrient statement is unsafe without soil testing.
Khadar is newer floodplain alluvium, whereas Bhangar is older alluvium on higher terraces; bhabar is a coarse porous piedmont belt and tarai is the wetter belt downslope.
The printed names bhabar, tarai, bhangar and khadar describe geomorphic/alluvial settings rather than four universally uniform soil taxonomic classes.
Loam is a balanced mixture of sand, silt and clay; sandy loam, clay loam and silty loam reflect the dominant fraction while retaining mixed texture.

Red and yellow soils develop widely over crystalline igneous and metamorphic rocks under warm conditions; red colour is mainly associated with oxidised iron and yellow colour with hydrated iron forms.
Red-yellow soils are generally porous and may be low in organic matter and available nitrogen/phosphorus, but fertility varies by depth, texture and management.
Red-yellow soils occur across parts of the eastern and southern Deccan and adjoining regions; the printed 18.49% figure is historical and must be dated.
The book separates red/black and grey/brown subgroups using parent material, colour and iron oxidation; these are descriptive groupings, not modern national taxonomic orders.
Black soils are also called regur or black-cotton soils and are strongly associated with Deccan basalt, though black soils can occur on other materials.
Smectitic clay gives many Vertisols shrink-swell behaviour, deep cracks in dry periods and self-mulching surface aggregates.
Black soils retain water strongly but may have slow infiltration and drainage when wet; high clay does not mean all water is readily plant-available.
Black soils occur in Maharashtra, Madhya Pradesh, Gujarat, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu; the printed 15% national share is an older approximation.
Black soils may contain lime, magnesia, potash and iron but can be low in nitrogen, phosphorus and organic matter; local testing remains necessary.

pages.heading: Black-soil PYQ, laterite and forest soils

facts.claim: The printed TGPSC 2024 Group-II question tests black-soil statements: large national extent, basaltic parent material, strong water retention and iron content; it must be preserved with exam label and official-key verification.
Laterisation under intense weathering and leaching removes silica and bases and leaves relative enrichment of iron and aluminium oxides.
Laterite is not simply defined by high temperature and rainfall; drainage, parent material, duration and landscape position also matter.
Lateritic soils occur in high-rainfall parts of the Western and Eastern Ghats and plateaus; the printed 3.7% figure is historical.
Lateritic soils are often acidic and nutrient-poor because of leaching, yet can support plantation crops with appropriate management.
Forest and mountain soils vary with altitude, slope, vegetation, parent material and climate; they are not a single uniform soil.
The book prints a historical 18.04% extent for forest soils; modern mapping uses different categories and boundaries.
Podzolisation can occur under cool humid coniferous conditions, but podzols are not the universal soil of all Indian forests.

pages.heading: Arid, saline-alkaline, peaty and marshy soils

facts.claim: Arid soils occur in dry regions, are commonly sandy to loamy, low in organic matter and may accumulate calcium carbonate or salts; properties vary with irrigation and drainage.
Arid-soil colour ranges from red-brown to pale; colour alone is not a taxonomic diagnostic.
Desert irrigation can raise productivity but poor drainage can cause waterlogging and salinity; canal irrigation is not an unconditional benefit.
Saline soil has excess soluble salts; sodic/alkali soil has excessive exchangeable sodium. The two conditions and their reclamation are distinct.
Salinity and sodicity arise through aridity, saline parent material or groundwater, seawater influence, irrigation and inadequate drainage.
Leaching plus drainage is central for saline soils, while gypsum is commonly used for sodic soils; reclamation must follow soil and water analysis.
Peaty and marshy soils contain high organic matter under prolonged wetness and oxygen limitation; they may be acidic and nutrient imbalanced.
The book lists occurrences in Kerala, coastal Odisha, Tamil Nadu, north Bihar, Uttarakhand and West Bengal; exact distribution needs current soil mapping.

pages.heading: Indian major-soil map

facts.claim: The printed map distinguishes forest/mountain, alluvial, red-yellow, black, laterite and arid soils at a small scale.
Small-scale national maps show broad patterns and cannot identify the soil of a farm or village; detailed surveys are required.
The map shows alluvial belts in the northern plains and east-coast deltas, red-yellow soils across much of the peninsular interior, and black soils in major Deccan tracts.
Lateritic belts are shown along humid uplands and parts of the Ghats, while arid soils dominate western Rajasthan and adjoining dry areas.
The map omits many local inclusions and transitional soils and must not be used to assign one soil to an entire state.

facts.claim: Soil erosion is detachment and transport of soil by water, wind or gravity; natural erosion becomes accelerated when human pressure exceeds soil-cover resilience.
Sheet erosion removes a thin, relatively uniform layer; rill erosion forms small channels that ordinary tillage may erase; gully erosion forms larger channels not removable by normal tillage.
Ravines are deeply dissected networks produced by advanced gully erosion; the Chambal region is a classic example.
Riverbank or riparian erosion removes bank material by channel flow and mass failure; Gangetic and Brahmaputra banks are important examples.
Wind erosion includes detachment and transport by suspension, saltation and surface creep; it is important in dry, bare, loose soils.
Splash erosion begins with raindrop impact; landslides are mass movements and should not be treated as identical to splash erosion.
Glacial erosion and coastal wave erosion are geomorphic processes, but the chapter should distinguish them from agricultural topsoil erosion.
Printed national area and annual soil-loss estimates are dated and method-dependent; they must be labelled as historical estimates rather than timeless facts.

Printed human causes include deforestation, overgrazing, unsuitable cultivation, shifting cultivation, excessive irrigation, poor drainage, mining, unprotected construction and unsuitable crop choice.
Strip cropping alternates protective and erosion-prone crops in strips to interrupt runoff or wind flow.
Stubble mulching retains crop residues to protect the surface, reduce evaporation and raindrop impact and support infiltration.
Contour tillage and contour bunding align operations or barriers across the slope to reduce runoff velocity and soil loss.
Terracing shortens effective slope length but requires design, outlets and maintenance; poorly designed terraces can fail.
Basin listing creates small basins or furrows to capture rainwater in suitable dryland settings.
Water harvesting stores runoff for beneficial use and can support recharge where geology and design permit; it does not guarantee recharge everywhere.
Slope management should match land use to slope, soil and erosion hazard; the printed 1:4 to 1:7 range is not a universal threshold.
Afforestation, agroforestry and controlled grazing maintain protective cover, but species and stocking must suit local ecology.

pages.heading: Conservation-method diagram

facts.claim: The printed diagram illustrates strip cropping, stubble mulching, contour tillage, contour bunding, terracing, basin listing, water harvesting and slope-based land use.
Vegetative strips check wind and runoff, while residues reduce evaporation and surface sealing.
Contour tillage follows contour lines, whereas contour bunds are physical embankments; they are related but not identical.
Terraces reshape a slope into steps; basin listing creates intermittent storage basins without fully terracing the slope.
Mechanical and vegetative barriers can slow water and promote infiltration, but safe overflow is essential.
Slope-based land-use planning places cultivation on gentler land, pasture on steeper land and forestry/protection on very steep land, subject to local capability assessment.

pages.heading: Research centres, state soil extent and USDA Soil Taxonomy

facts.claim: The printed list assigns research centres to Dehradun, Chandigarh, Kota, Vasad, Agra, Ballari, Ooty and Jodhpur; institutional names and current mandates require verification before scoring.

The printed state-area table gives Uttar Pradesh 12.95, Punjab 12.25, Gujarat 12.14, West Bengal 8.50, Rajasthan 7.28, Maharashtra 5.34 and Tamil Nadu 0.04 lakh ha; the measure and source year are unclear and must remain historical/unscored unless verified.
The printed land-degradation box cites 2011-13 to 2018-19 monitoring and 97.85 million ha or 29.77% degraded land; exact wording must follow the cited atlas and year.
Soil Taxonomy is a hierarchical diagnostic system; the current highest level has 12 orders, not the book's incomplete nine-order list.
The book lists Inceptisols, Vertisols and Oxisols on this page; each order is defined by diagnostic properties, not simply by a one-line climate or colour description.
Inceptisols have weak to moderate horizon development; Vertisols have high shrink-swell clay; Oxisols are highly weathered tropical soils rich in stable iron/aluminium oxides.

pages.heading: Soil Taxonomy continuation and erosion map

facts.claim: The printed continuation lists Alfisols, Ultisols, Aridisols, Spodosols, Histosols and Mollisols; modern Soil Taxonomy also includes Andisols, Entisols and Gelisols.
Alfisols have clay-enriched subsurface horizons and relatively high base status; Ultisols are more strongly leached and base-depleted.

Aridisols are soils of arid environments with diagnostic subsurface features; Spodosols have spodic accumulation; Histosols are organic soils; Mollisols have a thick dark base-rich mollic surface horizon.
The printed India erosion map distinguishes gully/sheet, sheet, desert, shifting-cultivation, glacial, coastal and wind erosion belts.
The erosion map is schematic and uses older boundaries and categories; it supports regional pattern learning but not precise local hazard assessment.

pages.heading: Andhra Pradesh soils and red soils

facts.claim: Soil is a natural body formed by interacting parent material, climate, organisms, relief and time; fertile AP soils are not produced by parent rock alone.

The printed AP grouping gives red 65%, black 25%, alluvial 5%, coastal sand 3%, laterite 1% and problem soils 1%; these figures derive from an older undivided-state/legacy profile and must be dated and denominator-labelled.
Red soils are widespread in present Andhra Pradesh, especially Rayalaseema and uplands, but no district has only one soil type.
AP red soils develop mainly from crystalline rocks, are often sandy loam to loam, porous and variable in depth and nutrient status.
Printed AP red-soil subtypes include Chalka/red sandy soils and Dubba/red loams; local names and percentages vary among legacy sources.
Red-soil crops printed include groundnut, millets, pulses and oilseeds, but suitability depends on rainfall, irrigation, depth, pH and nutrients.

pages.heading: AP red, black, alluvial and coastal soils

facts.claim: The printed Chalka and Dubba descriptions distinguish coarser and finer red soils; exact local names should be retained but explained using texture and depth.
The book prints a 25% black-soil share and 65-80% clay; both are legacy generalisations and not universal for every Vertisol.
AP black soils have shrink-swell behaviour, strong moisture retention and drainage/workability constraints; they occur in parts of Kurnool, Nandyal, Palnadu, Guntur, Prakasam and other districts.
AP alluvial soils occur in Godavari, Krishna and Pennar floodplains/deltas, vary from sand to clay and support intensive agriculture where water and drainage are managed.
The printed 5% AP alluvial share is a legacy estimate; district reorganisation and classification changes require dated data.
Coastal sandy soils occur along the seaboard and are coarse, permeable and often low in nutrient and water retention; salinity and groundwater quality may constrain use.
The printed 2% forest-slope soil note and associated altitude/depth statements are broad descriptions, not statewide thresholds.

pages.heading: AP forest, lateritic and coastal soils and map

facts.claim: AP upland/forest soils are generally shallow to moderately deep and vary with slope, rock, vegetation and erosion; steep land is especially erosion-prone.
AP lateritic soils occur in humid uplands and hill tracts, are often acidic and iron-rich and may support cashew or plantation crops with management.
The printed 2% laterite and 1% coastal-soil shares conflict with page 301's 1% laterite and 3% coastal sand, demonstrating why the percentages must not be presented as simultaneous current facts.
Coastal soils may be sandy or saline and occur in discontinuous belts; lagoon, delta and beach settings differ.
The printed AP map uses pre-2022 district boundaries and a coarse four-category legend, so it must be labelled historical and supplemented by current APSAC district soil-resource maps.
The printed map's categories are red, black, alluvial and coastal-sand/other soils; local inclusions are not shown.

completion_state: Every recorded printed fact is linked to one or more chapter MCQs; printed tables remain preserved in the page ledger.
